title: Foods do not defile; violated women are not guilty
english: Foods do not defile us, holy pope, if the captives ate what their masters placed before them—especially since everyone agrees that the barbarians who overran our regions did not sacrifice to idols. The apostle says, “Foods are for the belly, and the belly for foods, and God will abolish both this and those” (1 Corinthians 6:13). And the Savior, who cleanses all foods, says, “It is not what enters that defiles a person, but what comes out” (Matthew 15:11). And as for the captive women being corrupted, with the barbarians committing violation against their bodies: But if a woman’s life had already been condemned before, because she walked after the eyes of fornicators, as it is written, then clearly her immoral disposition is suspect even in the time of captivity, and such women should not readily share in the prayers. If, however, a woman who had lived in extreme chastity and had shown her former life to be clean and beyond all suspicion has now fallen into violation through force and necessity, we have the example in Deuteronomy concerning the young woman whom a man found in the open country and, after forcing her, slept with her: “You shall do nothing to the young woman; there is no capital sin for the young woman, because just as if a man rises up against his neighbor and takes his life, so is this matter. The young woman cried out, and there was no one to help her” (Deuteronomy 22:25–27). These things, then, are so.

translator_notes: Greek copy-text: Documenta Catholica Omnia Canones GR.
This section covers Canon I; Canons II–XI follow in sections 2–11.
orientation: Gregory is writing to a bishop about how to treat Christians who were taken captive by barbarian invaders and ate food placed before them, and about women who suffered sexual violation at the hands of the barbarians.

title: Greed that profits from the invasion
english: Greed is a terrible thing. It is not possible in a single letter to set out the divine Scriptures, in which not only robbery is denounced as something to flee from and shudder at, but greed of every kind and every grasping at what belongs to others for shameful gain; and anyone of that kind is cast out of the Church of God. But that, at the time of the invasion, amid so much wailing and so many laments, some should dare to think that a time bringing ruin to all was for them a time of gain—that is the mark of impious men, hateful to God, whose outrageousness nothing could surpass. So it has been decided to excommunicate such people altogether, lest the wrath come upon the whole people, and first upon the very leaders who fail to look into these things.

For I fear, as the Scripture says, that the impious man may destroy the righteous along with himself (Genesis 18:23). “For fornication,” it says, “and greed—on account of these the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience” (Colossians 3:5–6; Ephesians 5:3, 6). “Do not, then, become partners with them; for once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—for the fruit of the light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth—testing what is pleasing to the Lord. And take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them. For the things they do in secret are shameful even to speak of; but everything that is exposed by the light is made plain” (Ephesians 5:7–13). So says the apostle.

And if some, while paying the penalty for their earlier greed, committed in time of peace, turn back to greed in the very time of wrath, profiting from the blood and ruin of people who have been driven from their homes, taken captive, or killed, what else is to be expected but that, pressing on still harder in their greed, they will heap up wrath both on themselves and on the whole people?

added_allusions.reason: μὴ συναπολέσῃ ἀσεβὴς τὸν δίκαιον, introduced by 'as the Scripture says'; Gregory adapts the LXX (Abraham asks God not to destroy the righteous with the impious)
πορνεία ... πλεονεξία, δι᾿ ἃ ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας
ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας
Μὴ οὖν γίνεσθε συμμέτοχοι αὐτῶν ... φανεροῦται, quoted almost word for word

translator_notes: Rubric of the canon collection left out (editorial, not Gregory's). ἐκκήρυκτος / ἐκκηρύξαι rendered 'cast out of' and 'excommunicate'; πάντα taken adverbially ('altogether'). οὐδὲ ὑπερβολὴν ἀτοπίας ἐχόντων read as 'whose outrage leaves no room for anything worse' and rendered 'whose outrageousness nothing could surpass'. Genesis 18:23 cited because Gregory introduces the line with 'as the Scripture says', but his wording adapts the LXX (there Abraham asks God not to destroy the righteous with the impious; here the impious man brings the righteous down with him); the English follows Gregory's wording. 'Fornication ... disobedience' blends Colossians 3:5–6 (δι᾿ ἃ ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργή) with Ephesians 5:3, 6; the rest quotes Ephesians 5:7–13 almost word for word. ἐπισωρεῦσαι ὀργήν may echo Romans 2:5 (θησαυρίζεις ὀργήν), but the verb differs; possible only, not cited. ἐπαγωνιζομένους τῇ πλεονεξίᾳ rendered 'pressing on still harder in their greed'. Accent θεία → θεῖα follows the source note; no change of sense.
orientation: Gregory condemns those who treated the invasion as a time to seize other people's goods, rules that they be excommunicated, and supports the ruling with Scripture on greed and the wrath it brings.

title: Worse than the sin of Achan
english: “Did not Achan son of Zerah commit a grave trespass concerning what was under the ban, and wrath fell on the whole congregation of Israel? He was only one man who sinned; did he die alone in his sin?” (Joshua 22:20). For us, at this time, every gain that is not our own but someone else’s ought to be counted as a thing under the ban. For Achan took from the spoil, and these men too now take from the spoil. But he took what belonged to enemies; these men now take what belongs to their brothers, and reap a deadly gain.

added_allusions.reason: Οὐκ ἰδοὺ Ἄχαρ ὁ τοῦ Ζαρᾶ ... μὴ μόνος ἀπέθανεν, LXX almost word for word; the story itself is Joshua 7

translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). The two opening questions quote Joshua 22:20 LXX almost word for word; the story itself is Joshua 7. LXX 'Achar son of Zara' given in the usual English Bible form 'Achan son of Zerah'. ἀνάθεμα rendered 'what was under the ban' / 'a thing under the ban' in both places so that Gregory's application of the word to present gain stays visible. The second question (μὴ μόνος ἀπέθανεν) expects the answer no. πλημμελείᾳ ἐπλημμέλησεν (cognate emphasis) rendered 'commit a grave trespass'.
orientation: Gregory compares such profiteers with Achan, who took from the devoted spoil of enemies, and judges them worse, since they take what belongs to their brothers.

title: Finders may not keep what others lost
english: Let no one deceive himself, nor plead that he found the goods; for not even a finder may make a profit. For Deuteronomy says: “If you see your brother’s calf or his sheep straying on the road, do not ignore them; you shall surely bring them back to your brother. And if your brother is not near you, and you do not know him, you shall gather them in, and they shall stay with you until your brother looks for them, and you shall give them back to him. You shall do the same with his donkey, the same with his garment, and the same with anything your brother loses—whatever is lost by him and you find” (Deuteronomy 22:1–3). So says Deuteronomy. And in Exodus this holds not only when someone finds what belongs to his brother but also what belongs to his enemy: “You shall surely bring them back,” it says, “to the house of their owner” (Exodus 23:4).

If, then, it is not allowed to profit from a brother or an enemy who in time of peace is careless, living in comfort, and neglecting his own goods, how much less from one who is in misfortune, fleeing from enemies, and forced by necessity to abandon his own goods?

an enemy's stray animal must be returned; Gregory's wording ('to the house of their owner') differs from the LXX as usually printed

translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). The print sets a Greek question mark after ἑαυτόν; the sense is a command and is rendered so. Μηδεὶς ἐξαπατάτω ἑαυτόν has the wording of 1 Corinthians 3:18, but it is a stock phrase and Gregory does not apply Paul's context; possible echo only, not cited. μήτε ὡς εὑρών rendered 'nor plead that he found the goods' ('the goods' supplied for English). Deuteronomy 22:1–3 LXX quoted. The Exodus line is named by Gregory and matches the content of Exodus 23:4 (an enemy's stray animal), but its wording ('to the house of their owner') differs from the LXX text as usually printed (ἀποστρέψας ἀποδώσεις αὐτῷ); cited as Exodus 23:4, English follows Gregory's wording. κυρίου αὐτῶν = their human owner, so lower-case. 'this holds' supplied for the Greek ellipsis. πόσῳ μᾶλλον ('how much more [is it forbidden]') rendered with the English idiom 'how much less'.
orientation: Finding something gives no right to keep it: the Law commands that lost goods be returned even to an enemy, and still more to someone who fled from the invaders.

title: Robbing others to make up for one’s own losses
english: Others deceive themselves by keeping other people’s goods that they have found in place of their own that were lost, so that, because the Boradi and the Goths have dealt with them as enemies, they themselves become Boradi and Goths to others. For this reason, then, we have sent our brother and fellow elder Euphrosynus to you, so that he too may give direction in the same way, following the practice we keep here, as to whose accusations ought to be accepted and who ought to be shut out of the prayers.
notes_covered: Greek copy-text: Documenta Catholica Omnia Canones GR typed print, p. 2, Canon ε´; read from the page image and matched against its text layer
ANF consulted only as sense check; not copied
translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). Βοράδοι καὶ Γότθοι = the Boradi and the Goths, the raiders of Pontus. τὰ τῶν πολεμίων εἰργάσαντο rendered 'have dealt with them as enemies'. συγγέρων rendered 'fellow elder' (fellow presbyter). δῴῃ has no expressed object; 'direction' is supplied for English, and the two clauses that follow are what he is to give direction about. Doubtful reading: Vossius' Latin ('ut secundum formam quae hic est, etiam ibi det similiter') suggests his Greek had 'there' (ἐκεῖ) where this print has αὐτός ('he too'); the English follows the print. ἐκκηρῦξαι τῶν εὐχῶν rendered 'shut out of the prayers'. No Scripture.
orientation: Gregory rebukes those who make up their own losses by keeping goods that belong to others, and sends Euphrosynus to apply the same discipline that Gregory's own church keeps.

title: Holding escaped captives by force
english: Something beyond belief has also been reported to us as having happened in your district—surely the work of unbelievers and impious people who do not know even the name of the Lord: that some have gone so far in cruelty and inhumanity as to hold by force certain captives who had escaped. Send some people into the district, lest thunderbolts fall on those who do such things.
notes_covered: Greek copy-text: Documenta Catholica Omnia Canones GR typed print, p. 2, Canon ς´; read from the page image and matched against its text layer
ANF consulted only as sense check; not copied
translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). The play on ἄπιστον / ἀπίστων ('unbelievable' / 'unbelievers') is kept as 'beyond belief' / 'unbelievers'. πάντως που ('surely, I suppose') is ironic: such things could only be expected of unbelievers. χώρα rendered 'district' both times. Κυρίου = the Lord (God), capitalised. σκηπτοί = thunderbolts; not a Scripture citation. Correction βία → βίᾳ follows the source note.
orientation: Gregory has heard that some in the bishop's district held escaped captives by force, and he urges that people be sent there.

title: Those who joined the invaders against their own people
english: Some were enlisted among the barbarians and, while captives, joined them in their attacks, forgetting that they were men of Pontus and Christians, and became so barbarous as even to kill their own countrymen with a club or a noose, and to show roads or houses to the barbarians who did not know them. These must be barred even from the stage of hearing, until a decision about them seems good in common to the saints when they have met together, and, before them, to the Holy Spirit (Acts 15:28).

added_allusions.reason: ἔδοξε ... τῷ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, the council formula of Acts 15:28 with the order reversed; a clear echo, not a quotation

translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). ἐν τῇ αἰχμαλωσίᾳ ἐπελθόντας is ambiguous ('attacked with them in the captivity'); read as Pontic captives who were enlisted and then joined the raiders' attacks, so 'while captives, joined them in their attacks'. ξύλῳ rendered 'with a club'; it could also mean a gallows or stake (ANF 'gibbet'); ἀγχόνη = noose, strangling. ἀκρόασις is the penitential grade of the hearers (see section 11), so 'the stage of hearing'. The closing words echo the council formula of Acts 15:28 (ἔδοξε τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν), with the order reversed by 'before them'; cited as a clear allusion, not a quotation; the English keeps 'seems good to … the Holy Spirit' so the echo stays visible. Χριστιανοί printed lower-case in the source; 'Christians' capitalised as English requires. κοινῇ correction follows the source note.
orientation: Christians who joined the raiders and helped them kill or rob their own people are barred even from the hearers until the gathered saints decide their case.

title: Raiding other people’s houses
english: As for those who dared to raid other people’s houses: if they are accused and convicted, you should not admit them even to the stage of hearing; but if they confess on their own and make restitution, they are to kneel in the rank of those who are returning.
notes_covered: Greek copy-text: Documenta Catholica Omnia Canones GR typed print, p. 2, Canon η´; read from the page image and matched against its text layer
ANF consulted only as sense check; not copied
translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial; it adds 'during the barbarian raid'). ἐπελθεῖν rendered 'raid' (come upon, assail). ἀξιώσῃς is second person singular, addressed to the bishop, hence 'you should not admit them'. ἑαυτοὺς ἐξείπωσι = declare themselves, confess without being charged ('confess on their own'). ἐν τῇ τῶν ὑποστρεφόντων τάξει ὑποπίπτειν as printed: ὑποπίπτειν names the kneeling grade (ὑπόπτωσις, section 11) and ὑποστρέφοντες are 'those who are returning' (the returning penitents; 'turning back' avoided because in English it can suggest falling away); not checked against a second Greek witness. Correction ἐαυτοὺς → ἑαυτοὺς follows the source note. No Scripture.
orientation: Penance for those who broke into other people's houses: if convicted, they are not admitted even among the hearers; if they confess and make restitution, they kneel with the returning penitents.

title: Keeping what the invaders left behind
english: As for those who found something in the field or in their own houses that the barbarians had left behind: if they are accused and convicted, they too are to be among the kneelers; but if they confess on their own and give it back, they are to be admitted even to the prayer.
notes_covered: Greek copy-text: Documenta Catholica Omnia Canones GR typed print, p. 2, Canon θ´; read from the page image and matched against its text layer
ANF consulted only as sense check; not copied
translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). The clauses are elliptical: the verb for the first ('are to be') is understood from section 8, and ἀξιῶσαι depends on an understood 'one should' (hence 'are to be admitted', not the weaker 'may'). ἐν τοῖς ὑποπίπτουσιν = among the kneelers (penitential grade, section 11); ὁμοίως rendered 'they too' (likewise, as in section 8). τῆς εὐχῆς = the prayer of the faithful, the standing-together grade; καί = 'even'. No corrections; no Scripture.
orientation: Penance for keeping what the invaders left behind: if convicted, they are placed among the kneelers; if they confess and give it back, they are admitted to the prayer.

title: No reward for returning what was found
english: Those who fulfill the commandment must fulfill it free of all greed for shameful gain, without demanding a fee for information, for rescue, or for finding, or whatever name they give these.

ANF consulted only as sense check; not copied
translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial; it spells εὕρητρα, the text εὕρετρα; text kept). τὴν ἐντολήν = the command to return lost property set out in section 4 (Deuteronomy 22:1–3; Exodus 23:4); not cited again here because the canon names no text. αἰσχροκέρδεια rendered 'greed for shameful gain', matching section 2. μήνυτρα, σῶστρα, εὕρετρα = fees for information, for rescue (salvage), for finding.
orientation: Those who return lost goods must not demand any reward for doing so.

title: The stages of penance
english: Weeping takes place outside the gate of the house of prayer. There the sinner must stand and beg the faithful who are going in to pray for him. Hearing takes place inside the gate, in the narthex. There the one who has sinned must stand until the catechumens leave, and go out from there; for, it says, “When he has heard the Scriptures and the teaching, let him be put out, and let him not be admitted to prayer.” Kneeling means that he stands inside the door of the church itself and goes out with the catechumens. Standing together means that he stands with the faithful and does not go out with the catechumens. Last comes sharing in the holy things.
notes_covered: Greek copy-text: Documenta Catholica Omnia Canones GR typed print, pp. 2-3, Canon ια´; read from the page image and matched against its text layer
ANF consulted only as sense check; not copied
translator_notes: Rubric left out (editorial). Usually judged a later addition, not Gregory's own words: Vossius notes it was absent from the Greek Nomocanon and found only in Cardinal Sirleto's manuscript; translated in full as printed. Names of the grades: πρόσκλαυσις 'Weeping', ἀκρόασις 'Hearing', ὑπόπτωσις 'Kneeling' (literally falling down), σύστασις 'Standing together', μέθεξις τῶν ἁγιασμάτων 'sharing in the holy things'. ἕως τῶν κατηχουμένων ('until the catechumens') rendered 'until the catechumens leave' (the dismissal is understood). ναός rendered 'the church itself' (the main hall, as against the narthex). The quoted line (ἀκούων γάρ, φησί …) is not Scripture and its source is unnamed; left uncited. συνίσταται after ἵνα (indicative, late usage) kept and rendered as 'stands with'. Corrections χρἠ → χρὴ and μετᾶ → μετὰ follow the source note.
orientation: A description, probably added to the letter later, of the stages of public penance, from weeping outside the church to sharing in the holy things.
